To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the genes responsible for the inherited cancer susceptibility syndromes are the same genes responsible for sporadic cancers; and that these genes play a key role in the pathogenesis of sporadic cancers.

the germline mutation in the cancer-predisposing gene is the initiating event in the pathogenesis of the disease, that the tumours that develop are characterized by the loss of the remaining wild-type copy of the gene, that the germlines of the patients are characterized by a high rate of loss of heterozygosity (LOH), and that the tumour suppressor gene product is often inactivated in the equivalent sporadic cancer.

the cancer-predisposing genes are tumour suppressor genes, and that the cancer-predominant phenotype is the result of the interaction of the germline mutation with somatic events that occur in the normal allele.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular basis of the inherited cancer susceptibility syndromes, and the analysis of how these genes contribute to cancer development.
the genetic and molecular basis of human cancer, and the application of this knowledge to clinical practice.
the identification and analysis of cancer susceptibility genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the inherited cancers are a heterogeneous group of diseases, each of which is caused by a specific gene mutation, and that each of the genes involved in these diseases has an essential role in the genesis and/or progression of the equivalent sporadically occurring cancer.

the genetic predisposition to cancer is an important factor in the genesis of many cancers, and that the identification of genes predisposing to cancer will lead to a better understanding of the mechanisms of cancer initiation, and may lead to the development of new therapies.

the genetic basis of inherited cancer susceptibility syndromes has been elucidated, but there is still much to learn about the biology of these genes, their function in normal cells, and their roles in tumourigenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are now in a position to identify the genes that are responsible for the inherited predisposition to a wide range of cancers, and to begin to understand how these genes contribute to cancer development and progression.
the identification of the genes responsible for the dominantly inherited cancers is an excellent example of the power of the genetic approach to the study of cancer.

we have made great strides over the past 2-3 decades towards understanding the genetic basis of cancer predisposition and, in the process, have gained valuable insights into cancer development and progression in general.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inherited cancer syndromes provide an invaluable resource for studying the biology of cancer, and for the identification of new targets for therapy.
the inherited cancer-suscessibility genes are often not only important for the development of their associated cancers, but also play important roles in other tissues.

inherited cancer susceptibility is a common cause of cancer, that the genes responsible are often the same as those that cause the equivalent sporadic tumours, and that the genetic basis of the inherited cancer-suspectibility syndromes can provide important insights into the molecular basis of the equivalent sporatic cancers.
